Attacks by the press are a certificate of honesty for their victims.
The press sentences people to death and disgrace, and the state courts carry out the sentence.
We have long since been living in the fulfilled here-and-now.
The eighteenth century, Rousseau, Goethe: all of it was a marvellous mythology of real existence in this world. But then unpleasant types crowd around the beautifully laid table, and it is all over.
Now the better beyond begins again.
Today’s practitioners of myth, such as Friedrich Georg Jünger, live on the leftovers and on dreams that come far too cheaply.
The poor devils who tried once more to take the fulfilled here-and-now seriously were quite rightly hanged and burned by the more experienced practitioners of this world.
Nietzsche was already among the latecomers.
The will to power is the will to a fulfilled existence in this world.
Arnold Gehlen is right when he says:
Every human type can fulfil its own ethos only when it rules. Everything else becomes moral degeneration.
The will to power is the will to potestas directa—direct power. But what is the will to potestas indirecta, indirect power, mere influence?
Is the will to indirect power somehow morally superior to the will to direct power?
To Hanns Winckelmann, together with the reply about the state secretaries:
Legality becomes something independent, something new.
Its foundation in “value-rationality”—in reason based on values—ceases to be interesting.
The law becomes the plan, and the plan becomes law.
Indeed, the plan becomes the constitution. And something more becomes clear: it is not the planners who rule. It is the rulers who plan.
Reason does not merely slide from the “value-rational” into the “purpose-rational,” from reasoning about values into reasoning about practical means and ends.
The very meaning of ratio changes completely as soon as it is transferred from value to purpose.

Do not forget: for an entire generation, not only technicians and industrialists but major philosophers as well demonstrated and celebrated the idea that the great advance consisted in functionalization—in moving from concepts of substance to concepts of function.
Remember Ernst Cassirer’s Substance and Function of 1910!
The civilized person thinks in functions!
And then, on top of that, “reason”!

Eduard Heimann recently gave a lecture in Berlin, in May, organized by The Socialist Century at the Wilmersdorf district office, with the following thesis: Because reason presupposes only one truth and one justice, the leadership at the summit of a rational society must become infallible.
He could have read that as early as 1921 in my book Dictatorship.
The rage directed at Ernst Jünger’s The Worker, and perhaps even more at my Concept of the Political, is the rage of a spa director at the doctor who diagnoses a case of plague in the resort.
I have made enemies of all the spa directors.
A society at once philanthropic and malicious.
I spoil the pleasure of a thousand harmless people.
A few factory owners developed worse heart trouble when they heard rumours of the plague case.
The diabetes of several bankers became alarming.

The season was in full flower, with delightful, long-awaited meetings in the most cultivated Marianne von Willemer style, and now it has all been ruthlessly trampled underfoot. So answer for yourself, you miserable criminal against human happiness!
Anyone who destroys the human feeling of happiness in a heartless way attacks the foundations of the social order and shall be outlawed as an enemy of humanity.
Tried in vain to decipher Däubler’s two “brother” sonnets, addressed to R. Pannwitz and me.
A magnificent flight and a miserable fall, directly beside one another.
Däubler is an ocean containing seaweed, plankton, octopuses, shoals of herring, fish spawn—but also magnificent dolphins.
Beside him, the early Rilke is a neatly polished goldfish bowl.
The Rilke of the Duino Elegies is a park pond.

Kelsen’s reasoning is designed to prove that Germany is a nothing in international law—truly nothing but nothing—and that only the Allies could create ex nihilo, out of nothing, an entirely different Germany with no connection whatsoever to the previous one.

The sight of this eager manufacturer of legal instruments of annihilation reminds me of the little helpers in the hell scenes of Hieronymus Bosch. But we have already experienced and survived destroyers, exterminators, erasers, and crushers of an entirely different scale. So let us leave him to himself.
In the seventeenth century, Spinoza took great pleasure in watching spiders and flies annihilate one another. It was his only recreation from thought.
You, as a great entomologist, might also be inclined today to enjoy this little spectacle. For me it produces a deep melancholy, and I prefer to look away.
Above all, horror at the autonomous logic of legality itself.
P. Humbert Clérissac, The Mystery of the Church.
Jacques Maritain’s preface is sprinkled with self-satisfied hints: Clérissac was a guest in Maritain’s home; Maritain served his Mass for a year, and so on.
Denis de Rougemont’s The Devil’s Share is very beautiful, delightful even.
Too beautiful and too delightful for its subject.
Perhaps this way of speaking about the subject is itself the ultimate form of cunning, taken to a level that cannot be surpassed.
Does he really risk coming into conflict with the devil as the devil appears concretely today?

Or does he remain with the triumphant exposure of yesterday’s devil and, when it comes to today, content himself with saying that some ancient devil is common to everyone and that everything is somehow the devil’s doing?
His maquis est une création posthume—his Resistance is a posthumous creation—as Gueydan puts it so nicely in his Thoughts of a Dean.
Now they all shout, with the malicious Niekisch leading them, that Nietzsche fathered Hitler.
Above all, Nietzsche’s Übermensch. But surely this Übermensch is the obvious consequence of believing in man as the maker of his own fate, a being who can raise himself beyond himself.
What, after all, is Shotwell saying that is any different?
Can an activist atheist want anything other than the Übermensch?
In 1923 Leon Trotsky wrote essays and gave lectures on literature and revolution in which he said:

“It lies in the direction of development that man will drive out everything dull, elemental, and unconscious; replace religion with science; and drive the unconscious out of politics through democracy, parliamentarianism, ‘and finally through the transparently clear dictatorship of the soviets.’”
“But the blind elemental force hangs most heavily over the economic sphere; that too will be driven out by socialist organization.
“But surely we did not do all this only to crawl on our bellies before the dull laws of heredity and capitulate before blind sexual selection.
“Man will rationalize this too and banish the dull fear of death.
“Man will make everything transparently clear and ‘create a higher social-biological type or, if one prefers, a superman.
“‘The average human being will rise to the level of Aristotle, Goethe, and Marx; above this mountain ridge, new peaks will rise.’”
That is how Trotsky ends his 1923 essay on revolutionary art and socialist art.
How much more fulfilled existence in this world there is in Wagner’s pessimism:
Nietzsche, then, was not merely a precursor of Hitlerism. He was also a precursor of Bolshevism.
Humanism: memories of youth, of our Latin-school days.
In Europe, the alliance between the Church and humanism can be explained through shared memories of youth and childhood from the pre-war world before 1914.
Now they all have a common enemy.

Christianity, which in Kierkegaard knew how to wipe the slate so completely clean and could appear so “inhuman,” now profits politically, in Karl Barth, from memories of the sermons delivered by the well-fed and securely established witnesses to truth of the nineteenth century.
Completely blind chance and the most exact, detailed planning are conceptual opposites, like emptiness and fullness.
The moment we begin to think, we find ourselves caught between such opposites. But people then group themselves into friends and enemies by using these patterns of thought.
